questions.knowledge_point: Integrating a Product of Trigonometric Functions Using Trigonometric Identities
questions.worked_solution:
We use the identity $\frac{1}{\operatorname{sec}⁡x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡x$ and $\operatorname{tan}⁡x=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\frac{1}{\operatorname{sec}⁡x}(3-\operatorname{tan}⁡x)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{cos}⁡x(3-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}(3\operatorname{cos}⁡x-\operatorname{sin}⁡x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =(3\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x)\,{|}_{0}^{\pi /4} \\  & =(3\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}+\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})-(0+1) \\  & =2\sqrt{2}-1\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
First, we multiply out the parentheses and then use the identity  $\operatorname{sec}⁡x=\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\pi /15}^{0}8\operatorname{sec}⁡5x(\operatorname{tan}⁡5x-{cos}^{2}⁡5x)\,\text{d}x & =8{\int }_{-\pi /15}^{0}(\operatorname{sec}⁡5x\operatorname{tan}⁡5x-\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡5x}\cdot {cos}^{2}⁡5x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =8{\int }_{-\pi /15}^{0}(\operatorname{sec}⁡5x\operatorname{tan}⁡5x-\operatorname{cos}⁡5x)\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this by substitution. Let $u=5x.$ Then $\text{d}x=\frac{1}{5}\text{d}u.$ 

Now, we fill the table for the limits of integration, according to the rule $u=5x.$

| $x$ | $-\frac{\pi }{15}$ | $0$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $-\frac{\pi }{3}$ | $0$ |

Therefore, the integral in terms of the new variable is

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}8{\int }_{-\pi /15}^{0}(\operatorname{sec}⁡5x\operatorname{tan}⁡5x-\operatorname{cos}⁡5x)\,\text{d}x & =8{\int }_{-\pi /3}^{0}(\operatorname{sec}⁡u\operatorname{tan}⁡u-\operatorname{cos}⁡u)\,\cdot \frac{1}{5}\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{8}{5}{\int }_{-\pi /3}^{0}(\operatorname{sec}⁡u\operatorname{tan}⁡u-\operatorname{cos}⁡u)\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{8}{5}(\operatorname{sec}⁡u-\operatorname{sin}⁡u){|}_{-\pi /3}^{0} \\  & =\frac{8}{5}(\operatorname{sec}⁡0-\operatorname{sin}⁡0)-\frac{8}{5}(\operatorname{sec}⁡(-\frac{\pi }{3})-\operatorname{sin}⁡(-\frac{\pi }{3})) \\  & =\frac{8}{5}(1-0)-\frac{8}{5}(2+\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}) \\  & =-\frac{8}{5}-\frac{4\sqrt{3}}{5}.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Integrating a Quotient of Trigonometric Functions Using Trigonometric Identities
questions.worked_solution:
We can rewrite the integral as

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\pi /10}\frac{\operatorname{cot}⁡5x}{\operatorname{csc}⁡5x}\,\text{d}x={\int }_{0}^{\pi /10}\operatorname{cot}⁡5x\cdot \frac{1}{\operatorname{csc}⁡5x}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Then, we use the fact that $\operatorname{cot}⁡5x=\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡5x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡5x}$ and $\frac{1}{\operatorname{csc}⁡5x}=\operatorname{sin}⁡5x$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /10}\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡5x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡5x}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡5x\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /10}\operatorname{cos}⁡5x\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this by substitution. Let $u=5x.$ Then $\text{d}x=\frac{1}{5}\text{d}u.$

Now, we fill the table for the limits of integration, according to the rule $u=5x.$

| $x$ | $0$ | $\frac{\pi }{10}$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $0$ | $\frac{\pi }{2}$ |

Therefore, the integral in terms of the new variable is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /10}\operatorname{cos}⁡5x\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{cos}⁡u\cdot \frac{1}{5}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{5}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{cos}⁡u\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡u{|}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}(sin\,(\frac{\pi }{2})-\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)) \\  & =\frac{1}{5}(1-0) \\  & =\frac{1}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Integrating a Quotient of Trigonometric Functions Using Trigonometric Identities
questions.worked_solution:
We can write the integral as

$$
\int \frac{{tan}^{2}⁡x}{8{sin}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{8}\int {tan}^{2}⁡x\cdot \frac{1}{{sin}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x.
$$

We then use the fact that $\operatorname{tan}⁡x=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}$ and $\operatorname{sec}⁡x=\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{tan}^{2}⁡x}{8{sin}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{8}\int {tan}^{2}⁡x\cdot \frac{1}{{sin}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{8}\int {(\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x})}^{2}\cdot \frac{1}{{sin}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{8}\int \frac{{sin}^{2}⁡x}{{cos}^{2}⁡x}\cdot \frac{1}{{sin}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{8}\int \frac{1}{{cos}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{8}\int {(\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x})}^{2}\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{8}\int {sec}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{8}\operatorname{tan}⁡x+C.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
We can write the integral as

$$
\int \frac{1-{cot}^{2}⁡x}{{cos}^{2}⁡x-{sin}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x=\int (1-{cot}^{2}⁡x)\cdot \frac{1}{{cos}^{2}⁡x-{sin}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x
$$

Then, we use the fact that $\operatorname{cot}⁡x=\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1-{cot}^{2}⁡x}{{cos}^{2}⁡x-{sin}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x & =\int (1-{cot}^{2}⁡x)\cdot \frac{1}{{cos}^{2}⁡x-{sin}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int (1-\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡x}{{sin}^{2}⁡x})\cdot \frac{1}{{cos}^{2}⁡x-{sin}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int (\frac{{sin}^{2}⁡x-{cos}^{2}⁡x}{{sin}^{2}⁡x})\cdot \frac{1}{{cos}^{2}⁡x-{sin}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\int (\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡x-{sin}^{2}⁡x}{{sin}^{2}⁡x})\cdot \frac{1}{{cos}^{2}⁡x-{sin}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\int \frac{1}{{sin}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

Now we use the fact that $\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}=\operatorname{csc}⁡x$ to express this as

$$
-\int {csc}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}-\int {csc}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x & =-(-\operatorname{cot}⁡x)+C \\  & =\operatorname{cot}⁡x+C.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}\frac{1-{tan}^{2}⁡x}{{cos}^{2}⁡x-{sin}^{2}⁡x}\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}(1-{tan}^{2}⁡x)\cdot \frac{1}{{cos}^{2}⁡x-{sin}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}(1-\frac{{sin}^{2}⁡x}{{cos}^{2}⁡x})\cdot \frac{1}{{cos}^{2}⁡x-{sin}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}(\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡x-{sin}^{2}⁡x}{{cos}^{2}⁡x})\cdot \frac{1}{{cos}^{2}⁡x-{sin}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}\frac{1}{{cos}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}{sec}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{tan}⁡x{|}_{0}^{\pi /6} \\  & =\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6})-\operatorname{tan}⁡0 \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}-0 \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}\end{aligned}

questions.worked_solution:
We can solve this by substitution. Let $u=\operatorname{sin}⁡3x.$ Then 

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=3\operatorname{cos}⁡3x\,⟹\,\text{d}u=3\operatorname{cos}⁡3x\,\text{d}x.
$$

Now, we fill the table for the limits of integration, according to the rule $u=\operatorname{sin}⁡3x.$

| $x$ | $\frac{\pi }{9}$ | $\frac{\pi }{6}$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ | $1$ |

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}{\int }_{\pi /9}^{\pi /6}\frac{3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{{sin}^{2}⁡(3x)}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{\sqrt{3}/2}^{1}\frac{1}{{u}^{2}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{1}{u}{|}_{\sqrt{3}/2}^{1} \\  & =-(\frac{1}{1}-\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}) \\  & =\frac{2\sqrt{3}}{3}-1\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
We can solve this by substitution. Let $u=\operatorname{sin}⁡2x.$ Then 

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2\operatorname{cos}⁡2x\,⟹\,\text{d}u=2\operatorname{cos}⁡2x\,\text{d}x.
$$

Now, we fill the table for the limits of integration, according to the rule $u=\operatorname{sin}⁡2x.$

| $x$ | $\frac{\pi }{12}$ | $\frac{\pi }{6}$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $\frac{1}{2}$ | $\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ |

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}{\int }_{\pi /12}^{\pi /6}\frac{2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)}{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{1/2}^{\sqrt{3}/2}\frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|{|}_{1/2}^{\sqrt{3}/2} \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2})-\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2})}{(\frac{1}{2})}) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\sqrt{3}) \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)}{2}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
We use the identity $\operatorname{sec}⁡x=\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}$ and rewrite the integral as

$$
\int \operatorname{sin}⁡x{sec}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x=\int \frac{1}{{cos}^{2}⁡x}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x.
$$

We can solve this by substitution. Let $u=\operatorname{cos}⁡x.$ Then 

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,⟹\,\text{d}u=-\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{{cos}^{2}⁡x}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x & =-\int \frac{1}{{u}^{2}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{u}+C \\  & =(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)^{-1}+C \\  & =\operatorname{sec}⁡x+C.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
We can solve this by substitution. Let $u=\operatorname{cos}⁡x.$ Then 

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,⟹\,\text{d}u=-\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x.
$$

Now, we fill the table for the limits of integration, according to the rule $u=\operatorname{cos}⁡x.$

| $x$ | $0$ | $\frac{\pi }{3}$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $1$ | $\frac{1}{2}$ |

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\operatorname{tan}⁡(x)\sqrt{\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}\,\sqrt{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\frac{\sqrt{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\frac{1}{\sqrt{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{1/2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{u}}\cdot (-\text{d}u) \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{1/2}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{u}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-2\sqrt{u}{|}_{1}^{1/2} \\  & =-2(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}-1) \\  & =2-\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
We use the identity $\operatorname{tan}⁡x=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}$ and rewrite the integral as

$$
\int \operatorname{tan}⁡x\,\sqrt{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}\,\text{d}x=\int \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}\,\sqrt{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}\,\text{d}x.
$$

We can solve this by substitution. Let $u=\operatorname{cos}⁡x.$ Then

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,⟹\,-\text{d}u=\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \operatorname{tan}⁡x\,\sqrt{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}\,\sqrt{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{\sqrt{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{u}}\cdot (-\text{d}u) \\  & =-\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{u}}\cdot \text{d}u \\  & =-2\sqrt{u}+C \\  & =-2\sqrt{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}+C\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem: Calculate $\displaystyle \int \dfrac{1}{\sin x}\left(\cot x + \sin^2 x\right)\,\textrm d x.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We multiply out the parentheses and then use the identity $\dfrac{1}{\sin x } = \csc x,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}(\operatorname{cot}⁡x+{sin}^{2}⁡x)\,\text{d}x & =\int (\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}\cdot \operatorname{cot}⁡x+\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}\cdot {sin}^{2}⁡x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int (\operatorname{csc}⁡x\cdot \operatorname{cot}⁡x+\operatorname{sin}⁡x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \operatorname{csc}⁡x\operatorname{cot}⁡x\,\text{d}x+\int \operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\operatorname{csc}⁡x-\operatorname{cos}⁡x+C\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Integrating a Quotient of Trigonometric Functions Using Trigonometric Identities
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We can write the integral as

$$
\int_0^{\pi/3} \dfrac{\sin x}{\cos^2 x}\,\textrm d x =  \int_0^{\pi/3} \dfrac{1}{\cos x}\cdot \dfrac{\sin x}{\cos x}\,\textrm d x.
$$

We then use the fact that $\dfrac{\sin x }{\cos x}  = \tan x$ and $\dfrac{1}{\cos x} = \sec x$ to express this as

$$
\int_0^{\pi/3} \sec x\tan x\,\textrm d x,
$$

which is a standard trigonometric integral. Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{{cos}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\operatorname{sec}⁡x\operatorname{tan}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{sec}⁡x{|}_{0}^{\pi /3} \\  & =\operatorname{sec}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3})-\operatorname{sec}⁡(0) \\  & =2-1 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Integrating a Trigonometric Expression Using Identities and Substitution
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We use the identity $\tan 2x = \dfrac{\sin 2x}{\cos 2x}$ and rewrite the integral as

$$
\int \tan{2x}\,\textrm d x = \int \dfrac{\sin{2x}}{\cos 2x}\,\textrm d x.
$$

Notice that the numerator of the integrand is proportional to the derivative of the denominator. So, we can solve this by substitution.

Let $u=\cos 2x.$ Then

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}=-2 \sin 2x \quad\Longrightarrow\quad -\dfrac 1 2 \,\textrm d u= \sin 2x \, \textrm d x.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡2x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡2x}\,\text{d}x & =-\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|+C \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|\operatorname{cos}⁡2x|+C \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|(\operatorname{cos}⁡2x)^{-1}|+C \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|\operatorname{sec}⁡2x|+C\end{aligned}
$$
